brussel-technical-architecture

Brussel — Technical Architecture

Overview

Brussel is a payroll, employment, and operational backbone built on a monolithic Phoenix application with clean context boundaries, a React Native frontend serving both web and mobile, and a suite of third party infrastructure providers handling regulated financial operations. The architecture prioritizes correctness and fault tolerance over premature optimization. Every architectural decision is made with the understanding that Brussel touches real money and real legal obligations.

Guiding Principles

Correctness over speed. Payroll that processes incorrectly is not a beta, it is a liability. Every architectural decision that trades correctness for velocity is rejected.

Monolith first. A well structured Phoenix application with clean context boundaries is easier to build, deploy, debug, and reason about than microservices at this stage. Extraction happens later if specific parts require independent scaling.

Compliance at the data layer. RBAC and permission enforcement lives at the API level, not the UI level. A UI that hides a button is not a security boundary. A controller that rejects an unauthorized request is.

Third party infrastructure for regulated operations. Tax calculations, ACH payments, bank linking, and signature validity are handled by licensed and compliant providers. Brussel never builds what a regulated provider does better.

Ambient intelligence. AI is embedded into workflows at the right moment. No chat interfaces, no explicit invocation. The product speaks when the product calls for it.

Backend

Language and Framework

Elixir + Phoenix

Elixir is chosen because the problem domain maps directly to its strengths. Payroll processing is inherently concurrent and isolated. Each payroll run must be completely independent from every other. A failure in one employer's run cannot cascade to another. OTP supervision trees provide this isolation natively.

Phoenix handles the HTTP layer cleanly with low overhead. Its context pattern enforces clean separation between domains without the operational burden of microservices.

Context Boundaries

The application is organized into six primary contexts. Each context owns its data, exposes a clean public API to other contexts, and never reaches into another context's database tables directly.
